recentItems.title: Foreign YouTuber fakes Aussie accent with AI to promote One Nation | ABC NEWS Verify
recentItems.description:
An ABC NEWS Verify investigation has uncovered a YouTube political commentator from overseas who is using AI to fake an Australian accent and promote One Nation to tens of thousands of people.

The account, Oceania Unfiltered, has accrued more than 3 million views and receives thousands of comments on its Australian and New Zealand political commentary.

The investigation also uncovered groups and pages sharing tips on generating social media content for profit, with one describing Australia as an untapped market.

Reporting by Jonathan Hair for ABC NEWS Verify.

recentItems.title: Diesel price surges as Middle East War continues | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
The Middle East war continues to drive up the price of liquid fuels, particularly diesel that powers our industrial, transport and agricultural sectors.  NSW Farmers' Grain Committee chair Adrian Roles says "it's not like we can pass on these additional costs because we sell into a global commodity market, so we're price takers as well." 

The price of diesel has soared since the conflict began and will accelerate because the base product - brent crude oil - is back above $US100 dollars a barrel. In addition, a global reduction in the capacity to refine diesel means the gap between the price of crude oil and what diesel costs is increasing. A specific problem is that the oil being disrupted is the most conducive to being turned into diesel but there are no plans to reduce the fuel excise. 

The shortage of diesel could get worse with US Senate Majority Leader John Thune sparking a discussion about a US export ban as prices in America surge too.  Earlier in the war, Australia did receive shipments from America. 

Before the conflict, transport companies would adjust fuel surcharges once a month, now they do this weekly. Neil Chambers from the Container Transport Alliance Australia says it's because of the volatility in fuel pricing. So it means that the increases in fuel costs have been passed through to the consumer much more quickly in the supply chain." 
All of which adds to inflation, something the Reserve Bank is worried about as well. The RBA's assistant governor Sarah Hunter recently said "over the last few weeks, the conflict hasn't reached a sort of sustainable resolution. We are definitely concerned about, therefore, what that means for fuel prices and the flow of crude oil and refined products through the global economy."  The RBA will meet to decide interest rates on September 28-29.

recentItems.title: Calls for Coalition to reveal migration plan after Labor unveils cuts | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
The boss of the country's biggest employer group, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Andrew McKellar told The Business Tony Burke's migration announcement is "a fairly responsible plan that's been put forward. It certainly doesn't do significant damage to the economy, but it does leave some gaps." He has taken particular issue with new working holiday makers ballot system. 

"Our concern would be the way this is proposed to be implemented will make it very difficult for regional and rural areas to attract backpackers to come out because the numbers in particular in that third year have been cut dramatically." He said. 

Andrew McKellar says looking ahead, where the government can legislate change, rather than relying on regulation it should, as this allows more certainty for business. "I think that's where the opposition comes in, so the government's now put its cards on the table. We would say it's also time for the opposition to come to the party to say what they would do and to explain why or why they wouldn't support legislative outcomes if that would provide greater certainty going forward." He said. 

As for whether the government has the net overseas migration target right, AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina says "if we can build 180,000 to 200,000 new dwellings every single year, then the magic number for migration would be 200,000 to 225,000 every single year."
